entry.evidence: processes controlling groundwater chemical evolution with reduced pumping are little known, and the impacts of reduced exploitation on regional hydrochemical changes are still unclear

steps.action: The authors pose the gap: how groundwater chemistry in the North China Plain evolves under the groundwater-exploitation reduction (GWER) project, and with what impact.
steps.quote: the evolutionary direction of groundwater chemistry is still unclear

steps.action: They propose a classification method that adds stable isotopes (δD, δ18O) to hydrochemical variables in hierarchical cluster analysis (HCA), to separate unconfined from confined samples where well information is unreliable.
steps.quote: this study attempts to propose a novel approach by integrating stable isotopes and chemical signals into the HCA method

steps.action: They collect 150 groundwater, 28 surface water and 38 precipitation samples in four campaigns (June 2019 to May 2021) and analyse major ions (ICP-OES, ion chromatography) and isotopes (laser analyzer).
steps.quote: A total of 150 groundwater samples and 28 surface water samples were collected in four sampling campaigns

steps.action: They check the reliability of the chemical data with ionic charge balance errors (within ±10%) and state the isotope analytical precision.
steps.quote: reliability of chemical data was checked by calculating ionic charge balance errors, which were within the acceptable limit of ± 10%

steps.action: They run HCA (Euclidean distance, Ward linkage) on log-transformed, standardized ions plus isotopes, and cut the dendrogram at linkage distance 20 into Groups A (N=93) and B (N=57).
steps.quote: the position of the phenon line at a linkage distance of 20 allows a division of the dendrogram into two groups of groundwater samples

steps.action: They check the clusters against mean well depth (90 m vs 263 m), the known shallow-brackish/deep-fresh contrast in the NCP, and isotopic differences consistent with Chen et al. (2003).
steps.quote: the information on sampling well depth also supports the aforementioned judgment

steps.action: They retain Groups A and B as unconfined and confined water, and claim the method can classify samples where geological data are scarce.
steps.quote: it is reasonable to identify Groups A and B as the unconfined and the confined water samples

steps.action: They fit the local meteoric water line, the local surface water line and the local groundwater line (slopes 5.5, 3.5, 5.9) to the δ18O–δD data.
steps.quote: the local meteoric water line (LMWL) can be defined as

steps.action: They compare the groundwater line with the meteoric line and with the upstream and mountain groundwater lines reported by Liu et al. (2019), and infer lateral inflow and surface water as the main recharge sources.
steps.quote: lateral inflow from upstream headwater basin was likely an important source of groundwater recharge

steps.action: They set δ18O against Cl− and compare the pattern with the expected trends for recharge, evaporation and mineral dissolution; they infer that mineral dissolution raises Cl−.
steps.quote: mineral dissolution contributes to the elevation of Cl concentration with no significant enrichment of isotopic values

steps.action: They classify hydrochemical facies with Piper diagrams for precipitation, surface water, unconfined water and confined water.
steps.quote: Therefore, the confined water was mainly Na-Cl and Na-SO4 types.

steps.action: They compare Pearson correlations, the (Na+−Cl−) versus (Ca2++Mg2+−HCO3−−SO42−) slope (−0.91 against the expected −1) and the chloro-alkaline indices with the signatures of dissolution and cation exchange.
steps.quote: signifying that the ion exchange alters the cationic changes in the groundwater

steps.action: They run PCA with Varimax rotation, extract three components (salinity-based, alkalinity-based, local nitrate contamination) and map the component scores by IDW interpolation.
steps.quote: These extracted PCs explain 77.87% of the total variance of the original multi-dimensional dataset.

steps.action: They set the GWER effect against natural seasonal water-level change as rival causes of the EC change in unconfined water.
steps.quote: To differentiate groundwater seasonal changes from GWER effects

steps.action: They design an overlay of EC change on water-level change, three zones, with a same-month, different-year comparison (Dec 2019 to Dec 2020) to remove the seasonal factor.
steps.quote: The effects of natural factors on water chemistry can be basically excluded by a comparison of both hydraulic and chemical signals

steps.action: They compare the overlap of EC decrease and water-level rise across the three periods: 89% (seasonal plus GWER), 69% (GWER alone), and 11% versus 89% in the falling-level season.
steps.quote: the overlap ratio of water level rise and the EC falling areas with the single impact of GWER is 69%, lower than 89%

steps.action: They check the attribution with the time series of mean EC over the four campaigns (Fig. 11): unconfined EC falls while confined EC stays stable.
steps.quote: the average EC values of unconfined water show an obvious downward trend from 2019 to 2021

steps.action: They ask which recharge or flow mechanism lowers the salinity of unconfined water.
steps.quote: So what specific factors contribute to the fall of salinity in the unconfined water?

steps.action: They list rival sources: local precipitation and surface water infiltration, lateral inflow, and upward leakage from the confined aquifer.
steps.quote: the recharge amounts from local precipitation and surface water infiltration are incomparable with lateral inflow and upward leakage from deep confined aquifer

steps.action: From Darcy's law they derive that lateral inflow should decrease as the water table rises and hydraulic gradients shrink.
steps.quote: lateral inflow flux from the surrounding areas outside the domain is estimated to decrease

steps.action: They exclude infiltration and lateral inflow by argument, leaving upward leakage from the confined aquifer.
steps.quote: The only possibility is that upward

steps.action: They derive that confined heads should rebound faster than unconfined levels, because the pumping reductions came mainly from deep wells (citing hydrographs in Liu et al. 2020b), creating upward head differences.
steps.quote: the confined water levels are anticipated to rebound faster than the unconfined water levels

steps.action: They test the leakage hypothesis with two multi-layer monitoring wells (Fig. 12): upward head differences of 5.4–17.3 m at Quzhou and 0.5–9.8 m at Qiuxian from June 2019 to May 2021.
steps.quote: two multi-layer monitoring wells with automatic data loggers recorded water levels to testify the previous hypothesis

steps.action: They examine the major ions in unconfined water over the four campaigns (Fig. 13): Na+, Mg2+ and SO42− fall stepwise, while Cl− and NO3− do not.
steps.quote: show a stepwise downward trend from the first sampling campaign (June 2019) to the fourth

steps.action: They keep the claim that GWER likely drives water-level recovery and the desalinization of unconfined water through upward leakage, with a negligible effect on confined water.
steps.quote: the ongoing GWER project was likely responsible for water level recovery

tree.answer: Hydrochemical change of groundwater under reduced exploitation (GWER) in the Heilonggang region
Ion and isotope concentrations are measured directly; aquifer membership, recharge sources and processes are not
Classify samples, find recharge sources, identify controlling processes and the GWER impact
GWER versus seasonal water-level change; infiltration versus lateral inflow versus upward leakage
Same-month interannual overlay isolates GWER; leakage predicts upward head differences
Conditions found, not set: a policy-driven pumping reduction observed in the field

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: Partly: four campaigns over about two seasonal cycles, and two monitoring wells
Partly: EC time series, ion trends and well heads agree, but the series is short and only two wells exist
GWER likely responsible for desalinization of unconfined water through upward leakage (best explanation)

end.claim: The groundwater-exploitation reduction project likely drives water-level recovery and the progressive desalinization (mainly Na+, Mg2+, SO42−) of unconfined groundwater, through upward leakage of low-salinity confined water, while confined water chemistry is little affected.

decisive_move.sentence: The overlay of EC change on water-level change, with the same-month, different-year comparison (Dec 2019 to Dec 2020) meant to remove the seasonal effect, is what lets the authors attribute the improvement in unconfined water quality to GWER.

gates.evidence: The four sampling campaigns and the existing monitoring wells were not directed by a stated hypothesis; the upward-leakage hypothesis was formed after the EC data and then checked against well hydrographs that could have shown downward gradients (p. 13). The overlay association (69%) is reported without a statistical test or a stated threshold (p. 12). No analysis was fixed in advance; the phenon line was placed after the dendrogram was inspected (p. 6).

imports.item: Hierarchical cluster analysis with Ward's linkage (Ward 1963) and Euclidean distance
Principal component analysis with Varimax rotation (Kaiser 1958) and the eigenvalue >1 criterion
Inverse distance weighted interpolation in ArcGIS 10.1
ICP-OES (Perkin-Elmer Optima 5300DV) and ion chromatography (Dionex ICS-2500)
Liquid Water Isotope Analyzer (Los Gatos Research)

limits: The supplied XML text contains only figure and table captions, so all body quotes come from the PDF text; symbols such as δ and ion charges are garbled there and were avoided in quotes. No review file was supplied; the acknowledgements thank reviewers, but no review sequence can be coded. Inference: the validation of the HCA classification is partly circular, because δD and δ18O were inputs to the clustering and then cited as further justification. Well-depth ranges of the two groups overlap (Group A up to 360 m, Group B from 50 m; Table 2). The authors admit that the time series is short and that the classification method remains to be tested in other cases (p. 14). Inference: the overlay percentages are not tested statistically. The exclusion of infiltration and lateral inflow rests on argument, not measurement. The leakage evidence comes from only two wells. Sub-claims and their statuses: the classification method is capability_characterized at most, weakly, since no independent ground truth is used; lateral inflow and surface water as the main recharge sources is best_explanation; geochemical controls (dissolution, cation exchange, nitrate) are best_explanation; the negligible effect on confined water is best_explanation.

disagreements.target: Routine practice of classifying groundwater samples by sampling well depth or screen depth
disagreements.support: The authors argue that farmer-reported well and casing depths are unreliable estimates and propose the isotope-plus-chemistry HCA instead.
disagreements.quote: the reliability of the sampling well basic information is often unconvincing

disagreements.target: Previous multivariate studies clustering groundwater using only hydrochemical data (e.g., Cloutier et al. 2008; Rajmohan et al. 2021; Sunkari et [...]
disagreements.support: The authors note that earlier work clustered spatially on chemistry alone and neglected vertical aquifer assignment; they add isotopes to the clustering.
disagreements.quote: [...] efforts focused on the spatial clustering of groundwater chemical evolution by only using hydrochemical data

alternatives_considered.chosen: HCA on chemistry plus stable isotopes to assign samples to aquifers
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Classification by sampling well depth or screen depth
alternatives_considered.reason: Well information is often an intuitive estimate by local farmers

alternatives_considered.chosen: Log-transform the chemical parameters except HCO3− and the isotopes, then standardize
alternatives_considered.reason: Chemical parameters are highly skewed; HCO3− and the isotopes are near normal

alternatives_considered.chosen: Exclude EC and pH from the HCA

alternatives_considered.reason: Ward's method produces the most distinctive groups

alternatives_considered.chosen: Phenon line at linkage distance 20, giving two clusters
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Other cut levels and numbers of clusters (not named)
alternatives_considered.reason: Two groups yield the most satisfactory results with distinct geochemical and isotopic signatures

alternatives_considered.chosen: Same-month, different-year comparison (Dec 2019 to Dec 2020) to isolate the GWER effect
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Adjacent-season periods (Jun to Dec 2019; Dec 2020 to May 2021) that include seasonal change
alternatives_considered.reason: Comparing the same month removes the effect of natural seasonal factors

alternatives_considered.chosen: Upward leakage from the confined aquifer as the cause of desalinization
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Local precipitation and surface water infiltration; lateral inflow
alternatives_considered.reason: Thick unsaturated zone and deep water table limit infiltration; Darcy's law implies lateral inflow decreases as gradients fall
